question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example is the E-major opening of the White Album
*Dear Prudence* / the same E–Bm opening that is quoted for *And Your Bird Can Sing*.

The verse is in E major. The first harmonic event heard after the guitar
figure is the tonic E major and the song then leaps a perfect fifth up to its
diatonic fifth degree, B minor. In a major key the diatonic fifth degree is
a minor triad, i.e. the v chord, the “minor-fifth’’ of the tonic. The
E – Bm I–v leap is the opening gesture of the song and is the same
tonic-to-minor-fifth jump that is normally illustrated with *And Your Bird
Can Sing* / *Here Comes The Sun* in D major – D→Am, i.e. I → v in the major
key. That is the characteristic Beatles I→v opening that is usually quoted
in teaching.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example is the opening of *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)* from Abbey Road.

The song is in E and the very first two bars are an E-major tonic that is immediately jumped to a B♭-major chord. B♭ is the ♭5 / diminished 5th / tritone of E, i.e. the “minor fifth”/flat-fifth of the tonic, and the move is a naked I → ♭V tritone jump before the riff settles back into E.

The same I → ♭V / I → v tritone jump is the one that is usually quoted for the group of late-’60s Beatles openers – it is the one most often heard in *Helter Skelter* / *Come Together* parlance, the E→B♭ opening of *I Want You (She’s So Heavy)* being the clearest instance of a tonic-to-(flat) fifth chord opening in the Beatles catalogue.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d say “Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown).” It’s in E major, and the opening acoustic pattern establishes the tonic E major before moving to B minor—the minor v chord—at the first vocal phrase (“or should I say…”). That tonic-to-minor-fifth shift is the harmonic gesture right at the start.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is usually quoted in this connection is the
Lennon/‘Come Together’ opening.

In the recording the song is heard in D  –  the D-major tonic is stated on
the first down-beat and the characteristic riff/bass figure is immediately
answered a tritone/four-and-a-half steps away on the G♭/♭V sonority that
functions in the literature on the track as the ‘minor-fifth’/flat-five
chord. It is that I → ♭V / I → b5 tritone root displacement, the tonic
being answered a minor fifth / tritone up, that gives the tune its famous
unresolved, “coming-together” jolt. 

That is the textbook Beatles tritone opening.  In a more literal I – v
reading the classic I → v, tonic to the minor fifth-degree opening is
the E–B m head of Please Please Me, E major tonic answered at once by its
minor fifth-degree B minor, the I – v jump that opens the record.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is normally quoted for this device is the one that everybody knows
from Come Together / the late Revolver-White Album period.

In the key in which the song is normally analysed, A minor / C major, the famous
McCartney/Harrison vamp is built round a tonic reference that is immediately
answered by a chord whose root is a tritone/minor-5th away from the tonic, the
bV / v sound which is the harmonic signature of the track. On record the bass
riff is heard as A → Eb, i.e. the tonic of the local minor tonality and the chord
a minor 5th/tritone up from it, the bV pivot that the song then sits on for the
whole verse.  It is that tonic → √bV/ tritone jump which gives the Come Together
intro its characteristic “wrong-note” lift and which is the Beatles’ best known
example of a straight tonic to minor-fifth / tritone chord jump at the very
start of a song.

The same device is often described in diatonic terms as the familiar I–v
opening of the early rock-and-roll material, the canonical Beatles example
being Twist and Shout / I Saw Her Standing There, E major tonic followed
immediately by the diatonic minor fifth chord B minor, i.e. I → v, the
classic tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree jump that launched the band’s live
repertoire.
